utterances.text: I think this means direct recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the courts enforced the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, those that were in force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Buntic I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one or two questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic. My name is Kovacic and I represent the accused Mario Cerkez. We have not had an opportunity to meet before with you. I would like to ask you, since we have you here as an expert, would you agree, Mr. Buntic, with a general statement that the municipalities within the organisation of -- within the administrative significance item of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia played an important role in the organisation of government in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I tried to point out that detail, that is, the federal constitution, the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the national defence law, the federal one, and the republic law on national defence, not only authorised the municipalities but also bind the municipalities to take certain defence measures in case of attack of war and even run, organise the Territorial Defence as a segment of all the national defence so it wasn't only the right, it was also a duty. Also the national defence law envisages a possibility of setting up a community of municipalities for a more efficient defence against any aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, in matters of defence, not only in other segments of life, in SFRY at the time, before the disintegration of the state, municipalities were an important link in this system; we can agree about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, just one more question to try to clarify one matter for those present here. Would you agree with me when I say that when the legal vacuum set in, when the central government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina fell through after it proclaimed its independence, but because of the -- because of the circumstances, of the conditions, it simply could not exercise its power because of the chaotic relations, because the whole system fell through. Following the Serb aggression, you told us today they took 70 per cent of the territory. When did the municipality then become -- the key moment which managed to maintain some kind of order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I'd say that of all the official, lawful, legitimate bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I have already said that all the official, lawful, legitimate bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina were blocked because the Serb Democratic Party quit those bodies. They simply could not take any valid decisions. They could not comply with the legal duties with regard to defence. So that only some of the municipalities complied with their legal and constitutional duties; not only rights, but also their duties. And in fact, that was the only way to preserve the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, or rather the remaining 30 per cent of its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness Buntic. I have no further questions. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, the tab number 5 which you presented, and as evidencing appointments of persons to the judiciary in Mostar, confirmed by President Izetbegovic, the date on that is what date? What is the date of that Sluzbeni List, which is the Bosnian official gazette? Would you tell me, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I know that some appointments in military and civilian courts were confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Permit me, please, then, just to tell you that what you have presented us shows a date of Friday, 18 September 1992. You yourself saw this particular document. You were aware of these appointments, having seen the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not learn it in this way, because at that time we did not have any communication with Sarajevo, nor could we get the official gazette from Sarajevo. It was physically impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then how did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I learnt it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, say, in 1994, maybe 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out and ask you if you had read the same -- or if you had been aware that in that very same Sluzbeni List, the very same official gazette which has been tendered into evidence here as Z216, if it's before everyone, the very same Sluzbeni List of 18 September 1992 announces the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, as I indicated, has been brought before this Court already in evidence. At the time you learned of these appointments, were you also informed about the same Sluzbeni List having this particular item?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said in my previous evidence that I received various issues of the official gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime in 1996. And I learnt about the appointments of the Judges when they were -- when they received the documents to that effect. The decision of the Constitutional Court, whether it had been served on anyone, I do not know. Not to me. And I already told you how I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oslobodenje has also been presented by you, at least an article in Oslobodenje. Did you read about the decision which was published in its entirety, in its entirety, in Oslobodenje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: You should distinguish between the different periods. The period of 1992, the October of 1992 period, was not a period when copies of Oslobodenje could be distributed outside of Sarajevo. It couldn't have been read outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Court had had a faxed copy sent to -- has in evidence a fax copy that was sent. Perhaps your correct personal delivery may or may not have been difficult. Did you have a fax machine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my office I did have a fax machine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not receive a copy of anything, so much as an announcement about this decision, whether it was Oslobodenje, a summary from Sluzbeni List, at the time it was handed down?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, would the persons whose names appear as being confirmed in Sluzbeni List to the bench in Mostar have learned about their confirmation, which was only published in Sluzbeni List?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I said that the decisions on appointment are being delivered to the individual judges, as well as published in the official gazette. They are simply delivered to them, and I think that the same practice is also in force here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not understanding you. If a judge in Mostar can have a decision delivered to him or her from Sarajevo, or a Sluzbeni List delivered, why could you not have gotten the same medium afforded to you? It's just not clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I'm also not clear on what period you're referring to. I'm talking about the decisions delivered to the judges in 1994 and 1995, after Sarajevo was unblocked. And also I said that as a private lawyer, I ordered all the back issues of the official gazette in 1996, and I received them, and from those official gazettes I learned about the decision of the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking not about back editions. I'm talking about judges who would have needed to know that they were appointed or removed in September of 1992. How did those persons know that they could continue on the bench? What you've provided shows a number of appointments and a number of resignations. How would they have known about this, which was emanating from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we're talking about the same period. I'm talking about 1994, 1995, and obviously you're referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The entire question has revolved around several items which were published in the very same Sluzbeni List of 18 September 1992, and only that time period at this point. How would these persons have learned about their careers and decisions which affected their careers if you didn't know about decisions that affected your career? It's just not clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear about it either, because if I say that they learned about these decisions in 1994, you are -- you seem to want me to say that I knew about it in 1992, so I don't know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm really not sure that you can -- we're probably not going to get very far on this, but I find another point in this document, the Sluzbeni List, about the appointments that are confirmed by President Izetbegovic. The courts in Mostar, the high courts, were in existence already. These were courts that had been part of the legal structure of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, what President Alija Izetbegovic is doing in this Sluzbeni List is confirming appointments on territory that he still deems to be his sovereign territory; isn't that correct? It has nothing whatsoever to do with anything selected by Herceg-Bosna, nothing.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Izetbegovic had in mind there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your ordering the back editions of Narodni List, did you check through the November 1992 Narodni List to realise that the first judicial appointments, the very first judicial appointments made by anyone in Herceg-Bosna were in November 1992, not September 1992, or not earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you didn't check, or no, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: There are several questions involved here, so let's break them down. One of the judges in the higher court or military district court in Mostar did not work because they had been appointed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. They worked and they were appointed on the basis of decisions of the presidency of the HZ HB. And whether President Izetbegovic confirmed them or not would be something that they only learned subsequently, like I did. That's one thing. The presidency of the HZ HB did also appoint judges prior to November 1992. These were appointments of judges to regular courts but not to the military courts, because the decision of the military courts was only adopted on 17 October 1992, and the appointments of judges to the military courts could only have taken place after that, after they were set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you're not understanding my question. My point is that the only things that are published about appointments in Narodni List show after November 1992 for regular judicial positions. Not military ones; regular ones. That's point one. The second one is: These courts existed and President Izetbegovic was doing that which was his legal and elected right to do. He was appointing persons, was he not, to exist in courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I already said: I cannot know what President Izetbegovic had in his mind. What he thought, I have no idea. We know what he did, which is in the documents that we had in front. No, I do not speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Where is the document that shows these appointments come from Herceg-Bosna? You were able to produce this document. Where is the document from the country to which you belong?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: If that is necessary, I don't think that there is any problem to it being delivered. I think it was published in the official gazette of HZ HB. It's all in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it can be brought at some point later. That would be fine. Thank you. The political party to which you belonged, I'd like to just discuss it for a moment to make sure that it is quite clear that it is not related to the HDZ. It, in fact, was the Croatian Democratic Party. And who was the principal founder of that party, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The president of this party was another colleague of mine, Mr. Tomislav Zelic, from Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the original party, can you give a little bit of background about its platform, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The political platform of the party was the modern integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would be organised in a decentralised way. Since three different people lived there, it was to be organised into three cantons or three republics or three regions. That was, in essence, the programme or the platform of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Marko Veselica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Marko Veselica was the president of the Croatian Democratic Party which was established and which is active in the Republic of Croatia. But the Croatian Democratic Party was separately organised in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It had its own organisation and its own president, who was Mr. Tomislav Zelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the party at one time, was it not, of General Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This party has been viewed as more conservative, to use a conservative word, more to the right, than the HZ HB. What was it that attracted you to this type of party, to that platform?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That is your opinion, not mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issues on family and boundaries were central issues on the platform of the party; population control, issues like that. Was that something that you were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the central issues on the platform of this party was centrality of family and population control. This is described, essentially, in a book of parties in Croatia. It is taken from a book from Zagreb. Can you comment on why that would be attractive to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: For me, the family is the highest good that a man can ever produce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And population control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we're being helped in this case by hearing the witness' views on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I move on to one other thing. The three cantons that you discussed, they were based on ethnic divisions were they not, ethnic divisions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they based on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: They were based on the constitution of the former Yugoslavia and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both constitutions provide for certain rights and some of certain experiences. The federal Yugoslavia consisted of six republics and had six constituent groups, and Bosnia was -- had three ethnic groups and it should be divided into three cantons. It never says anywhere that those three cantons should have been monoethnic. You will never find such provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a comment about regionalisation of -- the term was regionalisation of some of the municipalities. You indicated that it occurred in 1992. I just want to ask you if you are familiar with information that came to this court through document Z12 which is a document dated 23 August 1991. In this document, Mr. Buntic, is the first evidence of regionalisation of the municipalities which were ultimately to be formed into HZ HB. Were you unaware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain then why you gave a date of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Here in this document, I don't see the year. I see the date 23 August, and also it states that this is a document produced by the Presidency of HDZ. And as I was not a member of that party, I was not in a position to know what their views were, and I don't see the year. The copy that -- in the copy that I have in front of me, the year is not legible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise for the quality of the copy. The English translation which was made from a proper copy does indicate 1991, and the very opening paragraph, if you note, does refer 6th of August 1991. So although you were not a member of the HDZ-BiH, you claim, can you tell me, please, how Mate Boban approached you to occupy such a high position? What was your relationship with Mate Boban that he would approach you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: When I gave evidence, I said that in the period between April and June, I was the deputy commander of the Brotnjo battalion. This is a unit that held the front line against the Yugoslav People's Army, the Serbian army from the 20th of December, 1991, until the 6th of June, 1992. The Serbian army, that is, the JNA and the Serbian troops were never able to break through that line that -- this was one of the first -- the first units established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was an unit which was actively involved in the liberation of areas east of the Neretva River in the operations between 6th and 25th of June, and I was the -- I came out of that campaign as a successful military commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an answer to my question? Is that why Boban approached you because you were a successful military commander? What about your legal skills?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I was an equally successful lawyer in the period between 1989 and 1992 with a law office which still has five lawyers and six administrative staff working for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mate Boban before you were given this position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: We would meet in Citluk because at the time, I'd say between February 1992 and February 1993, the HVO command was mostly in Citluk because of the position of Citluk, the proximity to Mostar, at somewhere between the end of January and the latter part of June 1992. So we would meet in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could answer how you met him initially, it would be helpful. Did you know him socially, personally, are you related?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No. We had not known each other before nor are we related in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe, please, how you were contacted for this position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I cannot recollect exactly, but it was a few days before the 15th of May, I think it was the evening we met in the Citluk municipal building at a meeting which was attended by Milan Lovric the then president of the Citluk municipality. In addition to him, Vinko Juricic, he is the president of the Crisis Staff, was there. They called me sometime after 8.00 at night. I was in the Brotnjo battalion command at the time. They called me up and they talked to me about the establishment of the civilian HZ HB, an executive body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and would I accept the position of the head of the justice department, that was their first offer, or to become the secretary of HZ HB, that was the second offer. That is how I was approached. I told them that I would accept it but that I will remain in my position until the end of the operations which were in progress, it was called the "June dawn" which included the liberation of the municipalities of Stolac and Ston, and I remained with my military duties until the end of the operations and only assumed the duties of the head of justice department after the operations were finished on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was your choice was it not to defer taking up the new position. You could have gone if you wanted to, could you not have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I could have assumed the position on the 15 May, but I, as I said, I chose to remain in my position at the time until the 20th of June. That is in my military position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could have remained a soldier, could you not have, and also assumed this position? You simply chose to stay at a front, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remained on the front line as a soldier until the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your comment about a discussion you had with Judge Trnka of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be common practice, for example, if you were meeting with a judge, a judge of a very esteemed body like the Constitutional Court, to break into a discussion about decisions that had been handed down by that court? Do you think a judge should take the initiative to tell you who, as a lawyer, should be informed about decisions that his or her court has rendered? Is that how you practice law in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. A judge in a high position, why is the head of the justice department on a lower position? I don't know if you confused the hierarchy here. The fact is that in the period of the 20th to 24th December, 1992, I worked with him on the development of the Vance-Owen Plan provisions and over the period of three days. He just didn't find it necessary to talk to me about this decision. I don't know whether it was his duty, but the duty of the court was to invite the parties to a discussion, and then following this debate, to deliver to them the decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a separate question. My question is: Why would you expect a judge to talk to you about a decision he has already handed down?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I told you that I hadn't even expected -- these copies of these decisions should have been delivered through the mail system, and this was not done or at least I am not aware of it having been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned early in your testimony that it was your opinion that the Croats were getting a bit of a, as it were, a raw or unfair deal because of their numbers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they were always doomed in your opinion, to be outvoted. Why did you not push for an alliance with the Muslims with whom the Croats and Muslims could have outvoted the Serbs on virtually any issue? What stopped you? What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: We were prevented by the constitution and the constitutional provisions which I quoted for you, that is, Muslims and Croats together did not have a two-third majority so they could not effect any constitutional changes if the constitution is what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the usual practice of coalitions and when there were joint presidencies and joint bodies, coalitions were the rule not the exception, and things could move. Why was it so difficult at that time? Why was your idea of a remedy to simply go out and set up a separate government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That idea never existed. The Croatian representatives in the BiH parliament advocated the preservation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the BiH parliament could adopt no decision because Muslims and Croats could not produce a two-third majority so they could not effect any constitutional changes, and the Serbian representatives, as I stated previously, boycotted it, not only the work of the parliament but also of the government and the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by separating themselves out of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you then suggesting that for all time, the Serbs got whatever they wanted, it was virtually impossible for any act or legislative action to be passed because of this? Did this persist for all 40-something years of the existence of the SFRY? Is this possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about the SFRY. I think we're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina here and the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the position of Croats in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that that is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... was this very short-lived institution, having just got its independence -- perhaps you can explain what was different in the way things -- very briefly because the court has had a fair bit of evidence about the history, but in terms of legislative success and legislative enactments, is there historically a record of great dissatisfaction by the Croats about this process?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: There is a major discontent of the Croats with the status in the former Yugoslavia, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did every law require two-thirds majority or was it just the law on changing borders that was required, that required a two-thirds majority? Can you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Don't talk to me about the change of borders. There was no mention of the change of borders. It was the change of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Buntic, may I stop you for a moment please. I have questions I'd like to ask you, and if you don't know the answer, I'd be grateful if you'd just tell me, but I'd like to get the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please do ask your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was, did every piece of legislation require a two-thirds majority or was it just legislation on the changing of borders in the republic? If you could help us with that I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: To change any constitutional provision, I am talking about constitution, not about laws. Perhaps it's the interpretation, excuse me. I heard you talk about laws and I talk about the constitution. To change any constitutional provision, a two-thirds majority was required. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was defined as the Communist and Socialist Republic in which the League of Communists was the only party and the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not change that provision because it did not have a two-thirds majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there no attempt to assist Bosnia-Herzegovina in its reformation of its system? Was it so optimal to pull away, abandon a country, a government of which you had been a part, you yourself, and that's part one? And so that I don't confuse you, and forgive me for making it a long question, but you yourself suggested that there was changes as of April 9 in the structure of the Territorial Defence, I mean, there was an attempt to deal with the need to change. Why did your particular group of people make a decision not to go along with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you explain this, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Because it was not physically possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I, in Mostar, could not go to Sarajevo. I physically had no access to Sarajevo. Physically, literally, Sarajevo was a city under siege which the Yugoslav People's Army kept under siege, and you could not enter Sarajevo. I couldn't go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are suggesting that the municipalities which were part of Herceg-Bosna would be justified in this type of separation because they were cut off physically from Sarajevo. Is that what I'm understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That's what I was saying all the time, that there was no physical communication of any centre with Sarajevo, not Mostar alone, but Bosniaks for the same reason set up districts of Zenica, Tuzla and Bihac so that those districts would take over decision-making in various matters and organisation of life in these territories, because the government in Sarajevo could not physically communicate with those parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about Kiseljak which was part of Herceg-Bosna, and where BH command was based. They had communication with the government in Sarajevo. They had fairly regular meetings with the government in Sarajevo. Why is it that one municipality of HZ HB was able to communicate other than physical distance? What's the difference? Kiseljak is what, 20 minutes on -- from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know, I do not know how somebody in Kiseljak communicated with somebody in Sarajevo. Yes, it's true, it's about 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo. They are very near. How they communicated, I don't know. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The personnel commission that you were referring to in point four of your summary, it was a de jure on paper commission, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think that there is a decision on the establishment of the commission so it did exist de jure but I do not remember that it ever meant in position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So de facto it really was nothing, but de jure it existed. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: My statement is that I do not recall it convening any meeting and nominating anyone to any duty. So that is my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then was it put on paper? What was the purpose in enacting it? What was the purpose of the exercise?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Why was the decision taken? I suppose one could explain it for a long time. Perhaps their presidency and government often debated why was this person appointed, why not that one; why two individuals from this one municipality, not from another one. And so perhaps it occurred to somebody that a personnel commission should be set up which then ought to take care of an equitable number of heads or deputies or whatever from all the municipalities. I suppose that was the purpose of the commission. Its chairman was Mr. Soljic. And the chairman convened some meetings under its statute. If the chairman does not convene such a meeting, then the commission simply does not meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then indicate to the Court -- because we were presented by both the Defence and by the Prosecution with a large number of legislation enacted by the Herceg-Bosna government. Can you tell us, please, which were real, which were actual ones that we should believe had a purpose and which were window dressing? In other words, there were a lot of de jure ones. How many of the ones that we know about would also have no real -- I know you don't know what we know about, but how many of the named official commissions and positions are really meaningless and, in fact, have a de facto side to them? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't really think I'd help you, because it would probably require -- and when I say this, I mean regulations, why did some regulations take root and why others didn't. It is easy to speak now why was something applied there and why wasn't, but think back to those times when there was no electricity, no telephones, when schools were closed down, where court did not work, when court buildings were destroyed. Go back to that time. It is not the time when 20 politicians would sit down and spend half a year discussing an act to be passed or not to be passed. It was a time when you had to take decisions on the spur of the moment because the next day it would be simply too late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That time period would have been -- I think you said it was up to June or so in 1992, right? I think that's what your original testimony was: up to about June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't put it that way. The war ended on the 22nd of December, 1995. Officially, on the 22nd of December, 1995 is when the end of the state of war was proclaimed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about conditions. I believe you earlier referred to conditions in Herzegovina, and you gave -- I'm sure I could ask to have it read back, if need be, but I'm confident it was a June 1992 or so date that things were really difficult. Do you confirm that or is there another date you'd prefer giving?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, true. I remember that the most difficult period was between the 3rd of April and the 20th of June. That was the hardest time of all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned that there was no electricity and that nothing was working.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask for a video, a very brief video, to be shown. There is a transcript available. I'm sorry. It is Z163.2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] This is -- However, life denies them. In the territory of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, life is more or less normal. There is buying and selling and trading in cars and televisions and stoves and refrigerators. But to explain this, one has to explain what is the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was established on the 18th of November. In Article 1 it says that it is a political, cultural, economic and territorial entity, so not a new state. But by the recommendation of those [indiscernible] organised units of the Croat people. The latest decisions from Grude following the same lines. It has become necessary to take individual regulations, that is, to fill in legal voids occurred by virtue of the decision of the authorities and bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are the laws on national defence, and this decision, regulation, was taken on the armed forces of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, the decision on rights and duties of members of the Croat Defence Council, decision of the takeover of the resources of the JNA, a decree on the transfer of ownership of property of the occupier and the decree on public enterprises. The adoption of these regulations and other regulations taken by the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna created the conditions for the normal unfolding of other forms of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First of all, I must apologise. This copy quality is not good and the original that I had seen is much, much better. You were much younger, Mr. Buntic, in that picture. But if I can ask you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The date on the newspaper -- if the audio people could possibly, just so we can date this, zoom back, I would appreciate it. Is it possible to go back to the frame where the newspaper -- very close up. It should read, I believe, the 7th or the 11th of July, 1992, and it's a Herzegovinian newspaper. Is it doable? Also in this video -- yes. Let's see if we can zoom up. We were able to do it yesterday. I don't know if we're able to do it today. Right over in the corner. I'm so sorry that it's bad quality. I can bring a later one in. I don't know if there's any way to actually get it to stop moving, but it does indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if there's any dispute about this, it can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm terribly sorry about this quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The currency that is shown as well is the Croatian dinar. Can you tell from that picture? Is it the Croatian dinar that's being exchanged? Were you able to observe that? The meeting that you were at was a meeting that was also attended by -- we saw Dario Kordic, and although I know that the video is terrible, Mate Boban was there. Were you able to observe that? Did you see Mr. Boban in the picture as well? Yes. Anto Valenta. And what was the purpose of that particular meeting in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought it was 1993, according to the transcript. The date given is 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It should be a year earlier. They're referring to a time a year earlier. July of 1993 would have been probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Somebody should have a look at this over the adjournment and we will see if that's correct. Perhaps the Defence could have a look too, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The date is incorrectly done. If the Court would permit me, I will try to get this corrected hereafter. I think it's an important piece of footage to see, and I'll get this corrected. It should be 1992, and we'll have to zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one point. If you're able to tell the Court what type of meeting that was and what it was you were discussing, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, it's eight years since, so I cannot say with certainty, but I think it was the meeting of the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna which adopted the regulations that are mentioned. So a decree on the armed forces and regulations that are mentioned here. I believe it was the meeting of the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna at Grude, in the hotel in Grude. I think that was the meeting and this was the -- these were some comments on the regulations adopted by that meeting. I think that's what it was about. So possibly, very likely, this is the tape of that meeting of the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The translation that I have indicates that was established on 18 November of last year, so that would have been 1991. So this is, in fact, 1992, and I will clear this up to the Court. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the points that was very strong was the suggestion that things were pretty good there, that things were running normally. Was there a difference among various municipalities in Herzegovina? I mean, Grude is close to -- they're all close to each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the period which preceded this one, so between April 1992, early April 1992, and June, end of June, 20th of June. And I said that in those areas, and I'm referring to the whole Herzegovina, there was no electricity, no water, no telephones. After the liberation of Mostar and Stolac, and it ended on the 20th of June, during those 20, or perhaps even 10 days, after that we already had electricity, we had water, and telephones too. So that the progress -- schools were closed until the 20th of June. All the civilians had been evacuated. Towns were empty. There wasn't a single civilian in any Herzegovinian town, because they were all shelled. They were all subjected to horrible artillery attacks. So there were towns without any civilians. In Herzegovina you couldn't find a man in civilian clothes. And that period ended on the 20th of June. After the liberation of a large territory, after the repulsion of the Yugoslav People's Army to some 20 kilometres east of the Neretva, the civilian life began to return. Somebody had to organise the beginning of work of schools; somebody had to give salaries to professors, to teachers, to soldiers, to the -- because the government in Sarajevo could not do that, physically; not because they didn't want to, but they simply could not. How to organise that life? How can children go to school?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to put you in any disadvantage and I will make every effort to get the corrected date to indicate that it, in fact, is July of 1992, if for just a moment you will accept that. Is it possible that within a two-month period of time there could be such a, as it were, a blooming in the desert, that things could be in such good condition as was shown in this video? This was -- I believe it was Radio -- or I'm sorry. If I can just ask the source of it. It was broadcast, though, I believe, from HTV. It's an HTV broadcast, Croatian TV broadcast.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. From this perspective I suppose it is very difficult to imagine certain situations; for me, for you, and for the Court, I suppose. In June, after two months of hell, I went on an official visit to Split and I saw lights and saw hot water. You don't know what that means. And so now probably it's very difficult to speak about that from this perspective. Even in those -- if we in those 20 days managed to set up civilian life, if we made some progress, if people came back, if civilians came back, if dozens of thousands of people could go back to their Siroki Brijeg, to their Ljubuski, to their Stolac, to their Mostar, dozens of thousands of people, isn't that a major step forward? For me it is, a tremendous step forward, a tremendous progress. If children could start school, that to me is a tremendous progress. If to you that's not a progress and if you don't see any progress in it, then I'm sorry; I'm sorry I came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, there's no need to talk to counsel in that way, Mr. Buntic. Yes, let's move on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we shall adjourn shortly. We have to take a slightly longer than normal lunch break. We'll come back at 2.45 and we shall then go on till 4.15. And I must ask you to bring the examination to a close before then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Five more minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a description in your summary of Herceg-Bosna and also the Patriotic League as a social institution. I believe it would have been point 17 and 18. Can you please explain that? If you could clarify how the government of Herceg-Bosna could be considered a social institution, given the types of institutions that were set up, it might clarify things for us. Can you explain the term, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: What else could it be? In my evidence, I already mentioned the number of constitutional provisions and laws, emphasising the duty of citizens, that they had to organise themselves and defend in case of occupation of the country. So that is one part relative to the defence of the country. And the duty of every municipality, by statute, to organise, to mobilise TO units from its territory and defend its territory. On the other hand, if we have military units which do not have civilian control, how do you imagine that situation? How can you have troops without civilian control, and unless you have official state institutions which are not blocked, which can work, and which can control those troops? The Bosniaks did the same thing. They set up their Crisis Staff through the Muslim Patriotic League and through the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that there was a necessity to establish a complete set of parallel institutions, which is, in fact, what happened, based on all the legislation we have seen, as a response to difficulties being experienced by the central government? Was that the perceived remedy, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No. And I've already testified about that too. The matter is as follows: If you have the possibility to -- if it is possible for the legal, legitimate civilian authorities to operate, then it's all right; if not, then it's anarchy. And any situation is better than anarchy. The civilian life needs to be organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that institutions which are set up by essentially a coup or a putsch are better than anarchy? Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't see why you claim that these organisations were set up by a putsch. They are fully constitutional, legal, and lawful categories. Madam, take the constitution of the Federation of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take the federal law, national defence, take the Republican national defence law, study them, and then you will see that these are no putschs, that this is simply compliance with the duties and rights prescribed by the constitution. Study the constitution. The all-national defence is chapter 7 in the federal constitution and chapter 6 in the Republican constitution, so study well those provisions, see what are the duties of municipalities, what they're bound to do in case of aggression and occupation. Do study that properly, and then you won't be talking about illegal actions, about putschs, about coup d'etat, and so on and so forth. Study the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are not to make speeches. You may well disagree with counsel, but, Mr. Buntic, would you remember that you're giving evidence to the Court. If you simply answer the questions, we will get on more quickly. If you disagree that it was a coup or putschs, you can do so firmly, but you must do so courteously, and also in as few words as possible. Yes, I think we will adjourn now. 2.45, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic in relation to the relationship of HZ or HR HB to the Republic of Croatia, you indicated that insofar as you were concerned, you had no dealings directly with any Croatian or Republic of Croatia legal person. Are you aware of the intricate nature of the relationship between the Republic of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, be it the community or the republic, that was set forth very clearly in a document which this Court has seen and only part of which I will ask to have shown to you. The number is Z2717 and will only be a very, very small part of it. The English would only be from pages 11 through 17 and if the Croatian is difficult to access I would be happy to give the usher my copy. The Croatian would be 5/1 through 6/3. To make it easier, I shall just quickly but hopefully comprehensively read to you when Ignac Kostroman refers to a meeting. Now this meeting, Mr. Buntic, is a stenogram taken from a meeting in President Tudjman's office in Zagreb held on the 27th of December 1991. Among the attendees were Mate Boban, Dario Kordic and a number of other people whose names you probably will recognise. The particular portion is a reference by Mr. Kostroman as secretary both of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and administrative secretary of the Croatian Democratic Union of BiH. The points that I want to ask for your familiarity with are a reference first of all to a meeting in Tomislavgrad held 23 December 1991, the minutes of which were read at this meeting of 27 December. Turning two pages to page 13 in the English, which would be item two in both English and Croatian, item two, point two, Mr. Kostroman reads from the minutes which, by the way, were signed off by Mate Boban, Bozo Rajic and Dario Kordic. He reads as follows, "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has once again confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on 18 November 1991 in Grude taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." The next point I'd like to raise is in item three. "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna recognises the full legitimacy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman as president of the Republic of Croatia and president of the Croatian Democratic Union to promote the interests of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna both among international factors and during interparty and inter-republic agreements on the establishment of the final borders of the Republic of Croatia. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna endorses the Croatian union of Bosanska Posavina in taking the same decision on behalf of the community." If you would go down to item four, please. "President Mate Boban, vice-presidents Bozo Rajic and Dario Kordic and secretary Ignac Kostroman are here by authorised to represent with the full legitimacy the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the meeting in Zagreb on 27 December 1991 (also in the future regarding further activities of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina.)" If you would please go to item 10 in the English, it is page 15. "The legitimacy of Alija Izetbegovic, president of Bosnia and Herzegovina to represent the Croatian people in public is hereby revoked because his recent actions or lack of them have facilitated and supported the Serbian army's attempts at establishing BH military training ground for the attack against the Republic of Croatia. Acting on behalf of the HDZ, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would not have given its consent for the extension of Alija Izetbegovic's term of office as president of the BH Presidency had there been regular personnel or personal consultations with the party." If you turn to the line just above item 14: "On the same day, the Presidency of the BH HDZ made official both Croatian communities." Item 14, "All Crisis Staffs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are ordered to increase the defence readiness of the Croatian people immediately because of the imminence of war in our territory. Crisis Staffs must remain in constant contact with the Crisis Staffs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and obey their instructions and orders." And then the last portion is simply the signature which would be in English on page 17 below item 19 signed by Mate Boban and vice-presidents Bozo Rajic and Dario Kordic. This particular document makes it very clear that the HDZ and, by extension, the HDZ BiH, controls, creates, runs Herceg-Bosna. Was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the first question. Before you ask the witness anything else, you'd better see if he agrees with that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That being the position that appears to be evident from the passages which I have read, is this consistent with your understanding of the purpose for which Herceg-Bosna was created?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does your understanding differ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I have presented my views as regards all official documents of the HZ HB, the acts and regulations that it adopted, as well as in all other documents the legally elected organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are recognised, and the HZ HB, all its bodies, its presidency and other bodies, advocated the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but with a provision to change and adapt certain provisions, to find a solution which would include all three ethnic groups, regardless of whether these would be three provinces, three cantons, or three republics. Those were the solutions which can be found in all legal official documents. I cannot comment on this document. I was not present at this meeting, as you can see from the signatories, and I was not present at any HDZ session. I don't think that I am the appropriate witness to comment on any decisions taken by the HDZ, because I was never present at any of their sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a high-ranking official of Herceg-Bosna, the question becomes: Was there an agenda, perhaps, of which you were not aware? You have indicated, earlier this morning, that that which is de jure is not always that which is de facto. Is it possible, Mr. Buntic, that you did not know the underlying goals of the state to which you had given allegiance? Is that possible, given what you have just seen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I only saw excerpts from a document. Since I was not in the meetings, since I have not been shown the entire document, I cannot comment on parts of it. I don't think that I'm the appropriate witness to do so. I don't have the entire document; I only have excerpts which are pulled out of context, and I never attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. However, a question could be put to the witness. The following could be asked of Mr. Buntic: Since you say that you are unable to comment on what has just been read out, you could at least tell us how you react, in the face of what you had stated earlier on. I think this is what is being required of you. You came with a certain amount of statements which were very direct, straightforward, and devoid of nuances as to Herceg-Bosna, as to its role and its creation and objectives, and you are now being given a document and you are being told this is what has been stated. So you are being asked to react, because, after all, you came here to testify. And you're not just testifying in one way; you are here to testify and tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: My response to this document -- if I understood you correctly, two questions were asked. First of all, did I know about this document. The answer to that question is no, I did not know about it. The second question is what is my attitude, what is my position to what you have just read to me. And I can tell you that again I did not know about this and such a document never appeared in any of the sessions that I did attend. So this was never an official policy of any body of which I was a member, that is, either of the HVO or the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, no de jure pronouncement came to your attention on this matter? Do I understand you correctly: No de jure pronouncement came to your attention on the facts contained in these passages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I was talking about the documents compiled by the presidency and the HVO as the executive body of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming the accuracy of what Ignac Kostroman has written here, does it shock you that so much power is given, for example, to Dario Kordic, to act well beyond the capacity of a legislator? Does that surprise you, as a lawyer, as someone who deals in de jure information, de jure practice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Again, this is a document produced by a party over which I had no influence, of which I was not a member, and whose meetings I never attended. So I have to come back to that. I can comment on the documents adopted by the -- produced by the presidency of the HZ HB and by the executive bodies of the HZ HB, but, please, I cannot make any comments on the party politics, party meetings, and documents which I had no access to. And I never had access to this document before, and I think that I have commented on my position on this document already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for a point of clarification. We accept that you were not a member of the HDZ. You were, however, a very high-ranking official of the entity which was created and run by the HDZ, albeit you were not a member; that is accepted. Does it concern you to know that this was the agenda of a body of which you were a very high official? That is my sole question. If you can answer it, fine; if you can't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I can answer the question. In a community, in a region -- we're not going to talk about a state -- there can be one, five, ten, fifteen different parties, and whatever transpires in a meeting of a party does not amount to a document of a region or state or some such entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, however, present at a meeting of Herceg-Bosna on the 29th of April 1993, I'm sorry, I just want to get the number of it. Sorry for fumbling, I had it in my hand. It's Z846, please. This meeting, if everyone has it, was held in Citluk on the 29th of April 1993. Your name is listed as being a participant and, in fact, the persons who summarised the highlights of the meeting have attributed to you on page four of the English translation paragraph. May I ask you, please, several questions about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness find the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me see if I can find it for you in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could interpreters have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would be happy to give the interpreters my copy if we could put my copy on the ELMO. Has the witness been able to get to the Croatian edition okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO? What page in the English is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the English, please, page two. Mr. Bruno Stojic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got it? Have you got the passage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where Mr. Stojic is speaking under Mr. Boras. First one comment that Mr. Stojic makes and he is speaking as one who is -- is he based in Herzegovina during the time period of 1992 to 1994? Is he at all times in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic is saying, "All reports from the field indicate that Muslims have not accepted the statement." Now the statement is referred to above. He then goes on to specify that they are attacking Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Konjic, et cetera. They are carrying out ethnic cleansing and a lot of allegations are following. My question is: How is Mr. Stojic, who is situated in the field, I'm sorry, situated in Herzegovina able to get these reports from the field? How does information manage to make its way back to him in Herzegovina yet it's more difficult for other people to get it in Herzegovina? Could you explain that or help us understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I will try. I believe that the military headquarters, that is, the defence department had separate communications systems, field telephones or something that I'm not familiar with. But I know that the military did have their own communication system which sometimes works, sometimes did not work. I think that the defence department at that period which is the period between 1992 and 1994 was better informed than other HVO departments, so there. But in what way...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accepting that, would not matters of great import that were received successfully by the defence department be communicated to the other ministries or departments of Herceg-Bosna, would it not be expected that if they got a piece of hot news that was important to the functioning or existence of Herceg-Bosna that it would be communicated? Would that be a logical expectation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. This was one of the ways for the defence department to transmit information it had and, as you can see, the head of the defence department informed the meeting, the question here. And the ministry of defence occasionally did issue or -- reports to the executive branch, the HVO on the political and other situation in the territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Recently when your colleague or your subordinate, Mr. Perkovic, was here, the Court heard evidence on the fact that from Busovaca, a dispatch about the creation of Herceg-Bosna found its way into the official file of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would that dispatch from Busovaca logically also have made its way up to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It depends on the period you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: July 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: July 1992, yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, a Mr. Ivan Saric, also on page two, speaks below Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we have that on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's on page two Mr. Usher and it's the passage where Mr. Ivan Saric is speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you know if it is Saric, or do you know? I may have a bad translation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivan Saric was a medical doctor. He is a physician by profession. I'm not sure, but I believe he was the assistant head for health services or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his role in a political meeting? Was he a representative also, a municipal representative?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was a representative of Tomislavgrad from where he originally came, but I believe that he was present at a meeting because of his influence in the health care affairs. That is what he specialised in in the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have any idea why he then might be commenting as follows: "What we succeed in defending with the military will be ours."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it like that in every war? Isn't it like that in every war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he was participating in this meeting in somewhat of a political capacity, that would be fair to infer from the comment? You were at the meeting, perhaps you could enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this meeting was not a meeting of the Presidency but of a broader circle of persons. I cannot recall it now, but evidently this was not the meeting of the Presidency. Perhaps it was an extended meeting to -- which brought together various officials but it is difficult for me to say, it was eight years ago. It is difficult to remember but I can I think that there were quite a number of people who were members of the Presidency and a number of people who were HDZ officials. But what the meeting was extended with, I don't know. Evidently there were more people here than in the Presidency or that part of the HVO. Evidently, there was a larger number of people than their number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the persons at the meeting was Mr. Anto Valenta, whom you know. I believe you also served on a commission with him, but I will ask you that in a moment. But if you'd look, the English would be page three. Mr. Valenta is speaking of events in Travnik and Vitez commenting that, "The Muslims are against the HZ HB, the Vance-Owen Plan and the Croats. The Muslims have opted for war. It is necessary to postpone the conflict with the Muslims, to wait for the decision of the UN Security Council, to wait for the reaction of America regarding the Serbs. Warned about the gravity and strength of the Muslim attack from Zenica on Vitez and Busovaca." At that meeting, why was Valenta indicating that the conflict was within the control of certain persons within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that they, in fact, could control when a conflict would erupt? Do you recall any further discussion about that point? It's an interesting point, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite get what you are driving at. If you are referring to this text here in Mr. Anto Valenta, as far as I can see, he issues a warning here to all those present at the meeting that the areas mentioned here, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca are absolutely encircled, that they are fully encircled. That is what he is warning about, as far as I can gather from this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help me understand my reading of it and maybe I'm wrong is that there is an element of control over when the conflict with the Muslims will end or begin, rather, and that element of control lies in the hands of some people at that meeting. That was my point. Have I misread that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I did not understand it in the same way as you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your comments are on page 4, and you're after, I believe, Mr. Bozo Rajic's comments. It's page 4 of the English. You are recorded as having said: Is of the opinion that many mistakes were made, first of all, regarding Muslim and Croatian refugees, with various consequences. You are quoted as -- or you are noted as having said that units will carry out part of the job, wherever necessary -- Central Bosnia, Konjic -- but you ask: How are we to retain the territory and manage it? You are thinking that a ceasefire must be arranged and negotiations held at once. You think that it is necessary to continue and intensify military, defensive preparations. You think that we, meaning the body gathered there, I presume, have to work specifically on the evacuation of the Croatian people in an organised manner from Zenica, as well as from other areas toward Travnik and Vitez, the Croatian provinces. You think that it is necessary to demand the recall of all foreign diplomats for whose presence we, I presume meaning the people at that meeting, or HZ HB, have not given our approval. You think that it is necessary to take an inventory of staff and that it is necessary to procure qualified staff to implement the Vance-Owen Plan. You think that this demands more aggressive, consistent, and better quality propaganda in HZ HB, RBH and the world. Could you comment, first of all, on the evacuation of the Croatian people. From where did you see the need to evacuate? When it says, "from Zenica as well as from other areas," which other areas were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: This needs to be viewed in the light of the fact that this meeting took place two or three days -- that is, in the wake of my visit to Central Bosnia. Zubak, Zuljevic and I went there together. We tried to tour Central Bosnia. We went up there, we took stock of the situation. We were using SFOR vehicles. And we barely escaped with our lives there, because fire was opened on these vehicles in Konjic. And this is not the first time; it was the second time to open fire on places where I was. That is an answer to the question why I never went to Sarajevo. When I was living in Sarajevo, fire was opened on a helicopter. And when we were coming from this tour, fire was opened on the vehicle that -- the SFOR vehicle that we were using. So we came to Zenica, I believe the St. Elijah church, because that was the only place we could get there. All 13 parish priests had been driven into the church. The president of the HDZ Zenica had been detained. We received the report that 30 people had been killed and 500 of them were in a camp in a mine. We talked in Zenica how to treat those people and whether those areas could be defended, that is, whether Zenica could be defended. Having drawn my lesson after all that happened, after the fall of Jajce, when all the Croats displaced from -- after the fall of Jajce ended up in hotels on the Adriatic, rather than in Central Bosnia, where they should have stayed and defended it, and I recommended to avoid that happening with Zenica. And if they were expelled from Zenica, not to marshal them towards the Adriatic or other countries, but to keep them in those territories. And that is why Travnik or Novi Travnik were mentioned as the closest places where these people should be kept. Women, children, and all those who were not able-bodied, thank God, should have been sent to other areas, but able-bodied men are not sent abroad when there's a war going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However -- and thank you for the explanation, but can you tell me, please: It says "from other areas."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears that there was not yet a need to evacuate. Am I correct from this? This was an anticipation on your part. You were thinking ahead at this point in time, which was, oh, 13 days after --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was already or you were anticipating something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: There was already a concrete danger. The HDZ -- the Zenica HDZ president was detained two or three days before that. His escorts were killed a couple of days before that, men who were escorting him. We received the report that some 500 men were in a camp in a mine and that there were already 30 people dead. After that, we could only expect an attack. I don't know what else could one expect. I believe that Zubak also spoke about that, because he headed the team which went to Central Bosnia. I don't know whether in this report which I have in front of me there is also Zubak's report. Can we please look at it, because he led the delegation; he was the head of the team which went to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date of your trip to Central Bosnia, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I told you, I cannot really remember after all the time, but it was on the eve of that session. Could it have been two or three days, I can't really remember, but it was right before this meeting. It was right before this meeting, a couple of days before it. That is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A point of reference, perhaps. Was it before or after the HVO massacre at Ahmici in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter of controversy. Was it before or after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think it was after that. That's what the date seems to indicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you, as a high-ranking official of HZ HB, were travelling in Central Bosnia, was there a discussion about what had happened at Ahmici, any version of the story, whether A attacked B or B attacked A? Was it discussed in the group in which you were travelling or with anyone with whom you met in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the discussion, if you can help us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The discussion -- we condemned it in the discussion. We went there all together. As I said, Mr. Zubak, Mr. Zuljevic, and myself. And Mr. Zubak was at the head of the delegation. And we knew that that indeed happened, that is, there was a conflict and that the outcome of that conflict was a large number of civilian casualties. I will repeat here what I said then, that I was sorry about that. I'm sorry for every civilian. I'm sorry for every man who dies in a war, in particular if it is a civilian or a helpless and defenceless individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as a person grounded in the law, feel the need to have this matter investigated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any measures toward that end?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. During that visit I also went to the courthouse and the prosecutor's office in Vitez. I spoke to the prosecutor there, saying that all the legally prescribed measures should be taken by the prosecutor's office in order to investigate all the circumstances and effects of what happened, that is, to investigate all the consequences of the Ahmici event. I spoke to the prosecutor -- let me just think. The name, the prosecutor's name escapes me, but it was the prosecutor in the military prosecutor's office, and he had his seat in Vitez. I'm trying to remember the name, but it simply escapes me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what representations were made to you by that prosecutor about what he or she would do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor knows what he's supposed to do. I suppose he knew what was within the realm of possibility, that is, to request a report from the military police, the police was to investigate all the circumstances, and then report to the military Prosecutor and then he would know how to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to assume that you asked to be kept informed about the progress of this investigation as you were clearly concerned about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one who was concerned about it. Others were concerned about it. That is, all three of us who were there were very much concerned about the incident and we requested that it be analysed and clarified, and I was the one who went to the military Prosecutor's office in Vitez and talked about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any further correspondence or communication with that prosecutor about the investigation from that point until today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: From that moment, I did communicate with the prosecutor. On about two occasions I called him by telephone so as far as we could do that and, he told me that he had ordered the military police to investigate all the circumstances of that case and that he had not received the report from the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of today's date, have you ever received any report or gotten word from that prosecutor or any successor prosecutor that the investigation was done with some result, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other point on here that I would ask you to clarify -- well, your comment or the comment that is attributed to you about recalling all foreign diplomats, why would the approval of apparently the officials of Herceg-Bosna be necessary for foreign diplomats to function, can you explain that, please, quickly I think because we are time conscious but...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't really. Perhaps we're talking at cross-purposes, they are not permanent diplomats, it's Bosnia-Herzegovinian diplomats in the world. There wasn't a single Croat amongst all the diplomats in the diplomatic core of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is what it means. Because here we are talking all the time what the Croat side has to do regarding the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan signed by Bosniaks and Croats, and that certain measures need to be taken in terms of the personnel policy, because we have to set up the government to set up the parliament, and to have a joint government. So have not two, but perhaps 200 or 350 men. And in the diplomatic missions at the time, there wasn't a single Croat representing in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
