So Bosnia-Herzegovina outside to the world was represented by one people only, and that is not the state of one people, it is the state of three peoples. And here so we're saying what the diplomatic -- what can be achieved by -- through diplomatic channels and the consequences of that because the world was receiving the information of one side only because the other side could not send out any information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I understand, if Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral sovereign nation composed of three constituent peoples has, as its representative, a Muslim or a Croat or a Serb, that Muslim, Croat or Serb could not represent the interests of the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: How could he if he's at war? Can you, when you are in a war, represent your enemy, represent his interests? It simply won't wash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a point earlier about the relationship of Herceg-Bosna to Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and you have suggested over and over again that, in fact, that Herceg-Bosna was a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can I ask you then, would it be a ludicrous assumption, if that were the case, then that Alija Izetbegovic would be considered a commander in chief of, let's say, the HVO and that Mate Boban could be considered a commander in chief of the ABiH if, in fact, they were an integral country? What would the influence of two separate leaders be over the opposite army, a parallel hostile army if, in fact, as it were as you represented it to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, we know what the situation was. We've already talked about it. We are talking about the situation when all three sides are in a conflict. Why -- how can I conceive that Alija Izetbegovic is the supreme commander of the HVO for a year and then that Mate Boban takes over. That would have been quite logical to me. Not because it's logical but because it is so prescribed by the constitution. The constitution prescribes that the supreme commander, that the president of the Presidency rotates every year, however, the constitution was violated and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic stayed in that position for three years. He could have held that post for one year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the usher show, just for a brief review, a document Z1385.1. It is in English only because it came in English only. It was sent initially in English only. What you have before you is a document which was sent to Brigadier Ramsey, Chief of Staff, UN command in February of 1994, 22nd of February, 1994. The content of it is partially relevant. What I'd like to ask you about, because it comes under, although it appears not to be the signature of Dario Kordic, it is on behalf of Dario Kordic by a person whose name I have difficulty discerning. The way it was sent, it perhaps was a -- simply typed up in somewhat halting English, but it refers to an incident in Busovaca which Zoran Maric from Busovaca municipality was charged to handle and which Mr. Kordic apparently thought fit to intervene and it is the ending on the last page that I'd like to ask you about. Again, it was sent to Ramsey. There was no comment, apparently it was just accepted and is signed off as vice-president of the Herceg-Bosna Bosnia parliament and assistant to the chief of staff HVO HQ command of Herceg-Bosna with a Travnik seal, Department of Defence. Is it common in your practice particularly as a legislative overseer to see someone use a legislative title on a document sent directly to the highest-ranking military person in the International Community, arguably, the content which is fairly petty but indicates a great deal of knowledge but on the ground matters. Is the ending, the salutation, the signing off common? Have you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: If you mean the seal, then, yes, but the signature here, I can hardly say anything. I'm not really sure what Mr. Kordic's signature is. I couldn't testify expertly about this. I do not think this is his signature. And the titles --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... his signature. It appears that someone signed on his behalf, but it came out under his name and it was delivered to BH command. The question is simply the way it is signed off with a title which, on a de jure basis, would seem bizarre. I think Perhaps I'm wrong, please correct me. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not common, it's not common.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Z341.11, please. This document is in both English and Croatian, I believe. Is there a Croatian edition, the Croatian will be provided through Narodni List. Quickly, if I may, this is a -- from Narodni List of September of 1992 it's a first issue and this concerns the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I would like to ask you to look at Article 3, please. "The HVO and the HZ HB and every HVO member are accountable to the Presidency of the HZ HB." Are you familiar with this provision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Earlier you indicated that Mr. Prlic would have been higher than Mr. Kordic. Mr. Prlic, however, was an officer of the HVO only, Mr. Kordic was a member of the Presidency. As a lawyer, do you see it perhaps differently if you look at this revision that as a member of the Presidency, Mr. Prlic would have been subordinate to -- as an HVO official, Mr. Prlic would have been accountable to Mr. Kordic as a member of the Presidency. Would that be how legal people in HZ HB would look at that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, de jure you may be right, but I know in England about Tony Blair, I do not know any member of parliament from the United Kingdom. I don't know any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That the HVO is accountable to the Presidency, but there are some 50 men who decide in sessions, none of them can take any individual decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In another case, a related case, there was testimony that was given that a Smiljko Sagolj, who was President Tudjman's legal advisor, if I am correct, in fact, drafted these provisions. Are you familiar with or are you aware of that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to the next document so we can finish. This would be Z2318. And I think it's comprised of two documents, it should be -- it was originally part of Z1345.1 just so that the registry knows and it was not tendered at that time but it was part of the -- it should be -- it is from March 1993, it is in Narodni List. This concerns, and I ask you this because perhaps you didn't have this in front of you when you were looking at the points 44 in your summary in discussing border crossing, and if you didn't have these things it maybe skipped your mind. But, in fact, Article 6 of the March document which talks about it is a decree on border crossing and in the border area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war. Do you recall this legislation generally as a -- as de jure legislation? Have you found it? If not I can give you my copy. It's in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I haven't. Is this document titled decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see, yes, it's translated as decree. It's Uredbu?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Uredbu in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: There is a number of decrees relating to these matters. Would you have a more specific --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Are you familiar, I'm sure you can't hold in your mind everything, but are you familiar with the border crossing decrees, and when you wrote your summary, had this simply skipped your mind? It would be page 122 if that will help you, 122, number 6, March 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of official border crossing within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina if this is what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you accept that this is, in fact, legislation of Herceg-Bosna. Article 7, just below the paragraph to which I was referring, and actually I'd like to ask you one quick question. On Article 6 before we move on, "Local border crossing are crossings used by citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to sojourn in a certain zone of the neighbouring state or by the citizens of the neighbouring state for crossing the state border in order to sojourn in a certain zone of the HZ HB." Is my reading of two separate, as it were, entities, HZ HB and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina incorrect as set forth here? There seems to be a reference to two separate entities. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No, not yet, not yet. I am trying to find it. I'd like to -- I would like to, if you can help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I would be happy to give you my copy first six and seven. They are circled in pencil, and I'd like to move on as quickly as I can, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've circled it for you, Mr. Buntic. Have you been able to read it through, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: So far as I can see, this is in reference of the border crossings of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and only the border area is here defined, and the rules within the border zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you draft this? Did you draft this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would look, please --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: These are decrees from the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Article 12, which would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you don't have it, I can give it to you right now in Croatian, to make it easy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall read it quickly. "Citizens of the RBiH carrying weapons and ammunition into or out of the HZ HB shall report the weapons and ammunition to the border police or the military police at the state border. Authorisation from the relevant administrative body of the HVO HZ HB shall be required when carrying weapons and ammunition across the border. If the weapons and ammunition from the foregoing," et cetera, et cetera. Do you recall this provision, again on matters concerning borders? Does this refresh your memory a bit on it? Just "yes" or "no" is fine, so I don't hold you up in this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: These are regulations from the area of finance, and I wasn't interested in that. But I think it refers to the border crossings into Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it refers to the confiscation of weapons. This is a routine matter done at any border crossing. I don't know why it would be any different in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps I'm not fully focused, but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the view is that it's another state. Moving on, please, Z2321. Because you've indicated you don't have as much familiarity with the financial aspects, I simply will ask you a quick question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if the usher would like my Croatian edition, I'm glad to give it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Otherwise you're more than welcome to this. My question to you is: This April 1993 section of Narodni List discusses essentially special legislation dealing with the import of goods from the Republic of Croatia. No other state appears to have any special legislation, but it does talk about Republic of Croatia. Are you familiar with this? Did you have anything whatsoever to do with the drafting of this, or was there any discussion about the special status for Croatia with the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed it in the meetings of the government, the HVO. Not once, but on several occasions. It is a fact that the goods imported from Croatia had special status, as did the goods imported from the Republic of Macedonia. I think that it only had a 1 per cent duty. I don't see why this is so special. The government did debate this, and I remember the debate. Croatia and Macedonia had a special status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Macedonia indicated in the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I only saw Croatia. Did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is mentioned. Perhaps if you peruse the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Z414.1. Mr. Buntic, this particular document is a document which is simply based on an instruction, as it were, that came under your hand. And because I do not have it in English, I will not ask certainly for it to be admitted, but it's a document I would just ask the usher to give to you, which talks about seals and stamps, official stamps and seals of Herceg-Bosna, just to show the witness, because this particular 414.1 appears to be based on his dealings with seals, coats of arms. Looking at 414.1, how often did you have to -- first of all, do you recognise this decision affecting the school in Bugojno or affecting these particular areas, among them the school and then Bugojno? Is this something you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the school in Bugojno means. I see that this is a decision on the manufacture of the seal, with the coat of arms, yes. It was issued by the Department of Justice. I did sign it. And yes, this document is a document that I personally signed and that falls within the jurisdiction of the Justice Department. But I don't know what was the reference to the school in Bugojno all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it has any particular significance. It's more that there is a special seal that existed for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And the particular instruction that you have in front of you -- which I don't think the Court would necessarily be interested in, but perhaps I can have it translated, if so -- indicates that there is a format, a description, a legal description of the seal, and that it, in fact, sounds very much of that which is used in Croatia, just by description. Is that fair to say? A coat of arms that bear a certain resemblance to certain Croat coats of arms, or the Croat coat of arms. It seems to be listed there. Is that a fair -- okay. Thank you. I'd like to ask you about three bits of legislation. It's part of Exhibit Z1464.4 from Narodni List of February 1994, and if it is not -- it's in -- it is a -- yes. It concerns, if the usher could show it to you -- I don't know. Was it distributed as part of the -- okay. Does everyone else have it? My question: There is a section on page 323B, the decision appointing Zlatko Aleksovski from Zenica. It says a graduate, I believe sociologist, and he's appointed as the director of the detention centre in Busovaca. Now, this legislation from Herceg-Bosna is quite specific about persons appointed to camps or detention centres and location. Was this typical of the practice in Herceg-Bosna as to specify names and particular camp locations? This would be Kaonik, presumably, in Busovaca. This Court has had a lot of evidence, so we don't need to get into the details of Kaonik, but just -- is it typical to list the appointment in this way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: This is the way how they were supposed to be nominated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the issue of camps in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, there is a second document that is behind it. It is a -- it is some commentary by persons from this Tribunal, made from interviews, investigative interviews, with Mate Boban, the late Mate Boban, and with Valentin Coric. Mr. Coric, on what is marked as page 8 of this four-page document -- it's 5, 6, 7, 8 -- comments that -- he mentions you, and he says: "There are laws governing all these offices and their functions. A representative of the division of public -- presumably public administration and of justice is Zoran Buntic. You can find him by the heliport." What was the heliport? Was that in Mostar? Is that where your office was? Was it in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Coric incorrect about the location of your office when he talked to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The office, that is, the official premises and the offices of the Justice Department and administration, were for a period of time in the Ero Hotel, and then the School of Machine Engineering. I don't know the exact number, but in one of those two locations. That is where the Justice and General Administration Department was always operating from, either the Hotel Ero or the School of Machine Engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at all times, from at least mid-1992 all the way through, let's say, the end of 1993, very early 1994 and February of 1994, were you at all times physically in an office in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Physically I was in the office in Mostar. And again, it was one of the two locations which I have just mentioned, either the Hotel Ero or the institute of the School of Machine or Mechanical Engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate very quickly how far the Hotel Ero or the other location where you may have had an office would be from the helidrome, the actual heliport? Just kilometres, if you can give an estimate.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Seven or eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at a document which is labelled from May 1994, it would be also a Narodni List. I just want to ask you a quick question about it. It's page 682 of number 18. It's a decision and it talks about some decisions of the Presidential Council of HR HB. It indicates that there's kind of a -- it looks like an expert panel or commission that was formed, and you were a member. It says: Zoran Buntic and Anto Valenta. Is that correct? Do you recall serving on this particular council or committee? And this was on cantonal demarcations, boundaries, borders of cantons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a document -- sorry. Pardon me one minute -- from an ECMM report, which is also part of a -- dated 26 February 1994. There appears the number R0133 -- I'm sorry -- 0131113. It is only in English, but I do want to ask you very quickly, where there is a comment: "According to Zoran Buntic, president of the Court Council of HR CR HB, the CR HB representatives on the Working Group Mostar has created another Working Group." Then it goes on, and then the comment is: "Mr. Buntic stated he does not understand why the map suggested by Pellnas ..." That must be Bo Pellnas, is that correct, Mr. Bo Pellnas? "... differs so much from the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, as the latter considered Mostar as the CR, or HR HB capital." Could you comment on that. You supported and worked on Owen-Stoltenberg, did you not? You favoured that plan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I said that we participated -- I think that in my examination-in-chief -- we did take part in it, and these are the people listed there. Anto Markotic [phoen] and Anto Valenta were there representing the Croatian side; Moca Borogovac, Mr. Trnka, and a third gentleman representing the Muslim side. We were working on the organisation of provinces further to the Vance-Owen Plan, and also the constitutional -- basic constitutional provisions based on the Vance-Owen Plan. After the adoption of the Stoltenberg Plan -- that is, both Croats and Muslims accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, and the Stoltenberg Plan was accepted by the Croatian and Serbian sides and rejected by the Muslim side. And I need to point out that the Croatian side was the only side who accepted all the plans put forward by the International Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But neither worked, neither came into being?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't see that the HZ HB is to be faulted for that, either myself or Dario Kordic, who was there, who was sitting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The one point that I wanted to ask: The division of Bosnia into three ethnic groups, as it were, under Owen-Stoltenberg, that is not substantially different, is it, from the basic cantonal division of the party, the Croatian Democratic Party, I believe, that you were initially -- or that you were a member of. In other words, the three divided ethnic groups was pretty much the pattern that you saw as appropriate for Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me for my personal position, I still believe that this was the best plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because we have four minutes, I want to just ask you: The post-Washington and, to some degree, post-Dayton, although it is not in our time frame of aspects of Herceg-Bosna, there is an Exhibit Z2821. I wanted to ask for your comment on it. And then there will be one last document after that and then we are finished. This document is only in English because it was a document from the United Nations mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina which, from time to time, selects interviews or open-source material that it considers relevant to its mission. And from Slobodna Bosna, of 26 January 1997, Kresimir Zubak was interviewed, and the point about which I'd like to ask you is on page three. Several questions are put to Mr. Zubak and there is a paragraph which begins, "A few days after the RBiH government ceased to function," meaning as part of a federation, "we passed the decision to dissolve the HB government and its ministries, but some other institutions and services have remained simply because we have not built these institutions and legislation in those fields at the federal level." And then it goes on to say, "As to the second question, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," meaning post-Dayton, "does not have state features as HR HB had -- police, army, financial, and customs -- all of which have been transferred to the Federation." Bearing that in mind that there was an abolition dissolution of the Herceg-Bosna structures required under both Washington and Dayton, I would ask you to turn -- or I would like to ask you about an allegation that was made about a Dayton violation that institutions in Herceg-Bosna were violating the ban on a customs policy. Are you familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not following it, and I think your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I finish that question simply by asking you to comment briefly on what the arrangements were for the abolition, the dissolution of the Herceg-Bosna institutions, so the Court can know that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The House of Representatives, and we're talking -- we're now referring to the HR HB, not the HZ HB. After the Dayton Accords adopted the decisions to transfer some of its authority to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, some to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HZ HB, which had been established on 18 November 1991, ceased to exist and had no more jurisdiction, and the new HZ HB was re-established as a cultural and social association, but this was only in 1995 or later. After the Washington and Dayton Accords, the House of Representatives transferred its powers partially to the Federation, partly to the central -- to the Republic, and partly to the cantons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there was a ban on any kind of customs activity by HZ HB and it were found to have been passed, it would be a violation. That would be a fair assessment, legally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I don't -- in 1995, 1996 there was no HZ HB; it didn't exist. HZ HB existed until 1993. It ceased to exist in 1993, when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna -- that was on the 28th of August 1993. So I don't know where the reference to HZ HB comes from. Perhaps it's the newly formed HZ HB, but it has no jurisdiction over any customs policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have the point. Yes, thank you, Ms. Somers. Yes, Mr. Naumovski. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, several times a question was asked how Bosnia was to be divided into three republics, three cantons, and so on and so forth, but Owen-Stoltenberg Plan and other plans all said that Bosnia consisted of cantons, that is, union of three republics, or some other way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: All plans for Bosnia-Herzegovina offered different solutions for Bosnia-Herzegovina, starting from Cutilliero's plan, which was the first one. It presumed a different internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina than the unitarian one through Vance-Owen Plan, Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, Washington, Dayton Agreements, which means that all the agreements which were signed, which were not signed, which were accepted and not accepted, and finally the Dayton and Washington Agreements did not divide Bosnia up; they simply offered a different solutions for its internal structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The question was asked about borders. We spent a lot of time on this, and in your summary, paragraph 44, the -- [Technical difficulties].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting the French translation. Mr. Naumovski, can you -- you were going to ask a question about borders. Would you ask it again, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very briefly, Your Honour. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, you told the Court explicitly that there were no official border crossings between the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the territories which were controlled by the Muslims. Is that so? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. I do not know of any border crossing official or any other within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision on border crossing which was shown you, you tell us, refers to border crossing between the state, between states, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It is, and in other parts, that decree mentions the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one detail. A part of the territory of the HZ HB is the border area of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the border crossing between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republic of Croatia are; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is in the narrow border belt towards the Republic of Croatia. For the most part, it has its longest border with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on. Z414.1, it's the seals and the description of the seals. A while ago you were asked about the Croatian coat of arms, which, we can agree, there is only one historical Croatian coat of arms, not several.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: True, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it also says the text of the seal needs to be first, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first line, and then Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and then whatever other text.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. As in all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is what you said during your morning testimony about the -- about HZ HB being a part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct, as confirmed by the seals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Anto Valenta was mentioned today. Now, just one side question. You must be following the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know that Mr. Anto Valenta is still a member of the border commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, regulations of borders with neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he is with Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A great deal was said today about the document that you didn't really have an opportunity to read through, and you believe that it is a document of the HDZ, it is a document of December 1991. So my question is: Were there different political options prior to the referendum held on the 29th of February, 1st of March, 1992 [as interpreted], among the members of all three peoples?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: One should probably say that in 1990 or 1991, all three peoples were discussing all possible options of the structuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina and possibilities of its survival, all three peoples discussed these matters, not only one people, all three peoples discussed it. And I believe that should be placed within this integration of Yugoslavia, all three peoples were thinking about that future and the future organisation on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, different options were on the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply a correction for the transcript, the referendum took place in 1992 rather than 1991, as it says here. So my question is: At the time when this document Z2721.1, when it was made during those discussions, that is, during that meeting Bosnia-Herzegovina was not an independent state, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was still, legally speaking, a part of Yugoslavia which was falling apart, which was disappearing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: In formal legal terms, yes, it was a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document Z846 it is a meeting in Citluk. The transcript shows that from Central Bosnia was -- that Central Bosnia was represented by Ivica Santic from Vitez, Pero Krizanac from Travnik, and Mr. Anto Valenta. Will you agree with me that Mr. Dario Kordic did not represent Central Bosnia at the meeting as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember if he was there, really. I don't remember. If he was present, I don't remember. I don't think so. I think he wasn't. I don't remember it was too long ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, that's logical, but the minutes speak for themselves. You also mentioned the investigation or rather your conversation with the prosecutor I will give you the name so perhaps that will jog your memory if that was the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I believe his first name was Marinko, but I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marinko Juncevic [phoen], isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Your Honours, I think that that will be all, thank you very much, thank you for your patience. Thank you, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I now raise a couple of matters after the witness is gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also have a matter, a 20-second matter, an application to add one witness to our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one witness listed for tomorrow, the first expert, Jankovic, is listed for Thursday. I made preparations to deal with him on Thursday, and I wouldn't be in a position to deal with him tomorrow. We may, therefore, run out of evidence tomorrow because tomorrow's witness won't be very long. Second point, if I am fortunate enough to be assisted by an expert on Thursday, and the same applies next week, by experts next week, may they sit in court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next point, I have now a report from the Dutch laboratory about the audio tape. It's a wider report than simply to deal with where the tape's been. It's a very comprehensive report and deals with more comprehensively than did Koenig, the Defence expert report, so I'm proposing to serve that today notwithstanding the fact that I wouldn't have to serve the balance of it. Maybe we could deal with the tape tomorrow if we otherwise don't have evidence to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On Thursday's second witness is a witness called Cavara who had been an affidavit witness. I didn't notice at the time we discussed him for reasons that I can explain, but he's never been on the Defence witness list. That came about in this way, if you recall, the first time we drew to your attention that there was an affidavit witness who was not on their list, although we'd had to face opposition to any additions to the list, the Chamber decided that for affidavit witnesses, the list maybe didn't apply. Cavara comes in as an affidavit witness and the Chamber's decision was that he shouldn't be giving evidence via affidavit, but it's still technically the case that he isn't a witness who's been added to the list. So that may be something that can be dealt with by Mr. Sayers. Not for this afternoon, but perhaps for tomorrow again, if we run out of evidence, the witness Dr. Pavlovic is, I think, due to come next week, and although the Chamber made a clear decision about whether he could give evidence as an affidavit witness, it invited the Defence to consider carefully whether he was going to be admissible for other reasons, and it may be, I don't know, it may be it's not possible but it may be possible to deal with that as an argument before the witness travels here tomorrow and perhaps they'd like to think about that. And in the same way, please, we now only have notification of witnesses up to the end of next week so we are now well short of a fortnight for witnesses. I hope you may have, please, a list of which witnesses are coming the week after next because our minimum entitlement is for two weeks of witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Responding to the last point first, Mr. President. Of course, I think we've been giving batting orders of every Wednesday for the two weeks in advance of that, and that's what we will try to do. I believe that the Prosecution has been notified of the witnesses for this week and for next week, and tomorrow I'll try to alert them as to the witnesses for the week after that, and I don't anticipate a problem in doing that. With respect to Dr. Pavlovic, we have considered the position. We have looked at the documents, and our conclusion is that he is basically simply being produced to authenticate documents. He's not being produced as an expert. He wasn't the personal physician for Mr. Cicak, who is the witness at issue; he simply sat on the work fitness assessment panel to make the decision that he should retire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible, though, if there is an argument that his evidence is inadmissible, that we hear it before he starts. So if there is a convenient moment tomorrow, we'll do that, and we'll also hear about the tape insofar as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If this is an extensive, report I'd like to consider it. And if I can respond tomorrow, then I certainly will, Mr. President, but if it's an extremely extensive report, we would appreciate a little bit of leniency in that regard. Tracking down the list, Mr. Cavara, obviously we're in the Court's hands. The Court required him to attend to testify in person. He's prepared to do that. We've made arrangements for him in the last few days, and he will be here -- I believe he's actually arriving tonight. So he will be here to be prepared in our office tomorrow afternoon and, if possible, if we run out of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And then the application that I mentioned is for a witness who'd last, in my estimation, about 15 minutes. His name is Ivo Marusic, and he will talk about the document that was introduced by the Prosecution in the cross-examination of Major-General Filipovic in our case and others. He is a gentleman who signed, as a chief of the Busovaca defence office, an award for Mr. Kordic, the order of King Petr Kresimir IV, with sash and morning star, and since that issue has been raised in our case, we would appreciate leave to add him to our witness list. Obviously, he's not going to affect the estimate that we've given to the Court regarding when our case may be over. In fact, if I might, I'd just like to update the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just on the matter of the award of the order, that's the sort of matter which I could have thought could be dealt with by agreement. If there's a statement from the witness or something of the sort, perhaps you might serve that, save the witness coming to say something which I can't believe there's going to be very much dispute about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would have thought not, and I will try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if you can resolve it in that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the closure of the case for Mr. Kordic, we are presently thinking that it would be closed during the week of July 17th. It might trickle over to the first day or two of the week after that, but I don't think so. I think it's the week of July 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So far you've been on target, so it's likely that you will remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless anything untoward happens. Talking of which, you have put in an application, which I'll deal with in this way, relating to evidence on the week of July 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will grant it for the 11th and 12th. That does mean that you've got to get through four witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think that will be a problem. There are two witnesses that are very short. They are in the nature of people that were incarcerated. One, I believe, was -- one's incarcerated in the music school. We hoped we could bring him earlier, but that didn't work out. The second witness talks about the discrete incident in the Kacuni checkpoint and was present when two people were killed at that checkpoint. The third person is the last of the so-called national case witnesses. Mr. Zuljevic, his testimony will be very short. And the fourth person is the person that the Court indicated it would wish to attend in person or to testify live, Mr. Stipac, and I would not anticipate that his testimony will be all that lengthy. Now, I'll also say that we're not sure that we can get Mr. Stipac there because he's relatively infirm and aged, but we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly for the 11th and, if necessary, finishing on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would not anticipate that that would be a problem getting all four finished. We've been fairly expeditious, I think, in direct, and we will continue to be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dealing with the witnesses, if you finish July 17th, the Friday is the 21st; that would leave two weeks before the recess beginning on July 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to bring it to the Court's attention, so we could have Mr. Cerkez start to put on his case immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. I think, Mr. Nice, we've heard from you. I'm sorry. Of course, we'll hear from you again. It's Mr. Kovacic's turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not really know if it's wise to take the floor now, because we are pressed for time. I could do it easily tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. But since you mentioned the calendar and the planning, I would have to follow up on that, but I do not know whether you think it -- would it suit you now or perhaps some other day this week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is getting on, but if you would have in mind that it seems that we'll be calling on you to start your case on the 24th of July. But if there's something you want to raise about that, do so at a convenient moment; it may be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will be very short tomorrow, probably three or four minutes. Since we raised that issue two weeks ago, I guess, I did some job and now I have some answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear about it later, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was simply going to say it's now obvious that, of course, the defence for Kordic knows the witnesses not only for the 10th of July but probably the witnesses right up to the end of case. We never provided less than six weeks, and I think as recently as November we provided the batting list up to the end of the case. In fact, it would assist us to have longer than the bare minimum for two weeks, and there's no reason why we shouldn't have, frankly, the whole list, and we'd ask the Court to order accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have that in mind. One final matter about the calendar. We have provisionally listed another case for the 4th of November. At the moment -- it may be possible to deal with the matter in another way, but at the moment we would have in mind to finish the evidence in this case before then. We will discuss this in due course and allow representations, but it may be sensible to have a break while we hear the -- as much as we can of the other case, a month or so. During that time, parties would be expected to get their final representations ready, and then in the run-up to Christmas we would hear any final evidence, rebuttal case, rejoinder, and hear final submissions. I mention that that, at the moment, is the sort of programme we have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear submissions, if need be. Yes, half past nine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 4.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
